article.title: Let Them Eat Touchdowns
article.author: Desi Cortez
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints are headed to Paris for Sunday's NFL alley fight, , bringing helmets, shoulder pads, cleats, television cameras, Wall Street sponsors, luxury fatcat suites, and football's favorite religion: **the almighty American dollar.** Meanwhile, beyond the stadium gates, France is burning, ablaze. Repeat, France is on FIRE! Students are protesting deteriorating schools. Workers are pissed, and I mean pissed, about the cost of living and erosion of public services. Everyday people, those souls who cook the meals, sweep the floors, teach the children, and keep somewhat civilized civilization up and running, are demanding something more than another bs sermon about personal sacrifice from politicians who never worried about the price of any damn thing.. And now, in an irony that has history laughing, the Steelers have canceled their planned fan celebration in Paris's Bastille neighborhood amid the unrest. The Bastille! Of all the places in France for America's billionaire-owned football circus to retreat from, it had to be the neighborhood named for the fortress whose storming helped ignite the French Revolution of 1789. You couldn't write a better punchline if Mark Twain, George Carlin, and Marie Antoinette's ghost shared a bottle of French cognac . Apparently, the NFL is happy to invade France for television revenue, but a party near the birthplace of revolution? Whoa, monsieur! That's a little too much history for cocktail hour. The fan celebration is canceled. The football game remains scheduled. Some festivities apparently matter more when security meets billion-dollar business. Let them eat touchdowns! Related: Europe’s Colonial Past Comes Home to Roost Hundreds of thousands of French citizens have taken to the streets: students, teachers, workers, the rank and file, the people who do the living, sweating, struggling, and dying while the aristocrats do the dining. Most have protested peacefully, although clashes with police, looting, and damaged property have supplied television networks with an abundance of dramatic footage. President Emmanuel Macron has condemned the violence and moved to restrict some demonstrations. Governments must protect people from violence. But protecting public safety cannot become an excuse for ignoring the grievances that brought people into the streets in the first place. Where are our decent schools? Affordable homes? Livable wages? Economic security? Our children's futures? And why, while everyone else is told to sacrifice, do those nearest the treasury always leave with their pockets full? The Hustle. Sound familiar, America? Different accents. Same damn con game. Their classrooms are overcrowded; ours are underfunded. Their workers feel squeezed; ours juggle jobs and bills while executives collect bonuses large enough to finance a small republic. Their young people wonder whether the future has room for them; ours graduate with debt , anxiety, and academic credentials that sometimes seem to come with an apology. One government calls it austerity. Another calls it fiscal responsibility . Either way, the filthy rivh get dirtier. They get cushioned seats at the banquet while working families receive the bill, instructions to tighten their belts, and an invitation to applaud the chef for serving nothing but the flippin’ aroma. France has its financial aristocracy. America has its highfalutin, country-club-dwelling, Wall Street-fed, Silicon Valley-bred Investor Class, forever confusing its bank balance with its moral worth. Different passports. Identical entitlement. Meanwhile, NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has discussed security with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and league officials have coordinated precautions with French authorities. The Saints have practiced in Versailles, the playground of French royalty, while the Steelers' Bastille celebration has vanished from the itinerary. Versailles, the Bastille, and billionaire football owners. Good Lord, history is writing the editorial itself. Which brings me to one question: “ Will America's football players bring anything to Paris besides retro uniforms and endorsement contracts?” Wouldn't it be something if these men, once students themselves (kinda, sorta, in a way maybe) demonstrated solidarity with French students, teachers, workers, and families fighting for a future that doesn't arrive with a foreclosure notice? Most of these pig-skinned gladiators can't spell solidarity if their lives depended on it, seriously. Perhaps a small patch stitched onto a jersey. A black armband. A warm-up shirt declaring WE STAND WITH THE PEOPLE. A raised fist during pregame ceremonies. Perhaps a knee during the French national anthem, not to insult the French people, but to insist that their flag belongs to the people marching beneath it, too. There's no shortage of gestures. Only, apparently, a shortage of institutional courage. Before somebody develops a patriotic rash, please spare me the stale pacifist sermon about keeping politics out of sports . The NFL has turned patriotism into a sponsored halftime attraction. It wraps itself in flags, honors military service, and sells reverence by the commercial break, but a player acknowledging struggling citizens suddenly becomes *political*? Please. That dog won't hunt in Paris, Pittsburgh, or Peoria. The league adores brotherhood, sacrifice, character, and leadership. Lovely words. They look terrific embroidered on a locker-room wall. But what good is brotherhood if it disappears when brothers and sisters outside the stadium ask for decent schools, affordable homes, and wages that last until payday? And who should understand better than professional football players? The vast, overwhelming majority grew up in Blue/Pink or no-collar-at-all communities, attended underfunded, subpar public schools, relied on teachers and coaches, and watched relatives work their fingers don ton their elbows to create opportunities they never dreamed of. Somebody once stood up for them. Now they have a stadium-sized opportunity to return the favor. Never, ever forget Colin Kaepernick. Branded, belittled, vilified, and effectively exiled from professional football after peacefully protesting racial injustice. One bent knee exposed how quickly a league selling courage by the truckload could become allergic to a man exercising his conscience. Kaepernick paid dearly, with his pro career. Today's players could also face repercussions: fines, suspensions, lost endorsements, perhaps even damaged careers. Courage is considerably less romantic when a mortgage, a roster spot, and a family's livelihood are on the line. But here's where the arithmetic gets interesting. One player kneeling can be isolated. Two can be threatened. But what happens when twenty, thirty, perhaps sixty players stand together? Will the NFL suspend half the Steelers and Saints? Fire them? Blackball an entire collection of athletes for showing solidarity with ordinary citizens? Related: Jaxson Dart, Trump and the NFL: When MAGA Politics Enters the Locker Room And suppose it does. Then what? Imagine the NFL’s billionaire owners punishing dozens of employees for publicly acknowledging people who aren't millionaires. Imagine the reaction across America, the conversations in barbershops, classrooms, sports bars, union halls, factory floors, college campuses, and family living rooms. Some fans would shout, "Shut up and play football!" That tired tune has played since Kaepernick took his knee. But others might ask why an employer's preferences should carry more weight than an employee's conscience. Perhaps those athletes could remind Americans that collective courage is contagious. The NFL is a multibillion-dollar empire sustained by players risking their bodies, brains, and futures. Owners hold the franchises, negotiate the television contracts, occupy the luxury suites, and collect proceeds. But without players, those billion-dollar stadiums become expensive parking lots, if not flea markets. Sixty players acting together wouldn't guarantee immunity from retaliation. But punishing a group is a different proposition from isolating one man. One raised fist can be dismissed. Sixty raised fists become a national conversation. And that conversation might travel farther than any forward pass. Perhaps Americans watching French students and workers challenge entrenched power would begin questioning our blind obedience to our own untouchable elites, who think democracy means permitting ordinary citizens to select which millionaire will explain why billionaires deserve another tax break. Ancient Rome understood the arrangement: ‘bread and circuses'”. Keep the masses entertained, distracted, sufficiently fed, and too busy cheering to notice who's emptying the treasury. No, honestly too uneducated, far too unenlightened to grasp the simplicity of “who” and “what” is screwing them. Twenty centuries later, the menu has improved: football, basketball, reality television, celebrity gossip, social media, wine, women, song, and enough electronic amusement to keep a civilization staring into screens while somebody, the Investor Class, quietly sells the country out from underneath it. Another way to say Investor Class…: The Champagne-Sipping, Tax-Dodging Trickle-Down, Kiss-My-Ass Aristocracy: that Highfalutin, Calculator-Hearted Gentry - Folks with a price for everything, a conscience worth nothing, an d a financial adviser where their moral compass ought to be. Nothing wrong with enjoying football. I do. But entertainment becomes a convenient sedative when people are expected to surrender their political voices at the stadium entrance. Give the peasants a touchdown, a beer, and a halftime extravaganza. Just don't give them ideas about demanding their piece of the rock. Nobody is asking the Steelers or Saints to tear down the Eiffel Tower, join street battles, or endorse looting. Supporting students and working families isn't endorsing violence. It's recognizing that broken windows make better television than broken promises, and powerful people understand the difference. Pittsburgh was built by steelworkers whose labor created fortunes for industrialists. New Orleans was built by working people whose music, culture, and resilience gave the city its soul. Its deep French connections make this meeting across the Atlantic especially fitting. Two working-class cities sending their football teams into a country where working people are challenging the powers that govern their lives. If an international sporting event ever arrived carrying a moral invitation, this one did. Imagine the cameras panning across players with fists lifted, armbands visible, heads high. Not another corporate awareness campaign. Not a charity photograph followed by champagne. Simply athletes acknowledging that people matter more than profit margins. Related: Putin, MAGA, Milei and the Demonic Monster Germany Thought It Buried Imagine that gesture crossing the Atlantic, inspiring conversations on campuses, in workplaces, and throughout neighborhoods. Americans might reconsider the difference between being entertained and being represented; between cheering for someone else's victory and standing up for their own future. The NFL can export football, television money, expensive merchandise, and enough corporate logos to wallpaper the Palace of Versailles. But can its players import a little French revolutionary backbone to America? Sunday's most memorable play might not be a touchdown or interception. It might be twenty, thirty, or sixty men remembering that before they were Steelers or Saints, millionaires or celebrities, they were somebody's children, students, neighbors, and members of the same working human family. Courage isn't only charging through a defensive line. Sometimes it means standing shoulder to shoulder when the people writing your checks would prefer you sit quietly. The aristocrats own the stadiums, the luxury suites, and the television contracts. But they don't own our consciences. And somewhere between the Bastille and the fifty-yard line, that might be the most revolutionary play of all: ordinary people standing together, staring the aristocrats in their privileged faces, and saying ENOUGH OF THIS GODDAMN NONSENSE! Liberté, égalité, hypocrisie! Will America's NFL gladiators raise their fists… or? Kiss their billionaire masters'..... Rings?
